title: Harden dangerous-command approval boundaries and preserve explicit bypass semantics
before: At parent 3ab7e2aa9190c32abd8f854f9f6a88ad9a2c3d0e, both dangerous-command entry points reread HERMES_YOLO_MODE from mutable process environment state on every invocation, so in-process code could enable the process-wide bypass after startup. Smart approval accepted any normalized LLM response containing APPROVE or DENY as a substring. Remote-content detection only recognized curl/wget pipelines whose shell token was directly sh or bash. Dangerous commands automatically allowed outside interactive and gateway contexts produced no audit warning.
after: At 4cb3eb03c750c902919906733b79220588ca5f16, process-wide YOLO configuration is parsed once at module import and both approval entry points consult the frozen value while retaining session-scoped bypass and existing hardline guards. Smart approval grants or denies only for exact normalized APPROVE or DENY tokens and escalates every other response. Remote-content detection additionally recognizes path-qualified sh/bash and bash -c forms. The legacy non-interactive, non-gateway auto-approval behavior remains, but each such approval emits a warning containing the matched description and a command prefix. YOLO tests patch the captured configuration value directly and continue checking bypass behavior in both approval entry points.
diff: The commit modifies tools/approval.py and tests/tools/test_yolo_mode.py (20 insertions, 10 deletions). It adds one import-time boolean, replaces two runtime environment checks, tightens two LLM-response comparisons, broadens one dangerous-command regex, adds one warning before a legacy auto-approval return, and updates three tests to patch the module-level captured value instead of mutating HERMES_YOLO_MODE.

title: Align approval and patch-safety decisions with the effective split filesystem policy
before: At parent c1ea3f95d13a851889d78a3d7ca7946162662c99, several core approval consumers still classified filesystem restriction through the legacy SandboxPolicy projection. Unmatched-command fallback and default execution approval derived allow/prompt behavior from legacy categories; shell, unified-exec, and intercepted-exec requests did not consistently supply the split filesystem policy to that decision boundary. Patch write safety also locally reconstructed readable and writable-root semantics instead of using the shared effective-access query. This allowed approval and patch-safety logic to diverge from the split policy carrying the actual filesystem carveouts.
after: At c2d5458d67714b9d92dfe18d8ebbb512001252d9, execution approval decisions consume FileSystemSandboxPolicy directly: restricted access requires or permits escalation prompts as appropriate, while unrestricted or externally sandboxed access follows the non-restricted path. The effective policy is threaded through shell, unified-exec, orchestration, and intercepted-exec call sites. Patch write eligibility delegates to the shared can_write_path_with_cwd query. Regression tests establish that legacy sandbox_mode configurations construct equivalent split filesystem/network policies and round-trip without semantic drift, and that a restricted split policy controls escalation even when the legacy projection says danger-full-access.
diff: The commit modifies nine core files (259 insertions, 76 deletions). It adds FileSystemSandboxPolicy to ExecApprovalRequest and intercepted-exec context, changes unmatched fallback and default approval classification to FileSystemSandboxKind, updates shell/orchestrator/unified-exec callers to pass the effective split policy, replaces manual patch-path calculations with can_write_path_with_cwd, and adds or updates regression tests for legacy-policy conversion, restricted approval behavior, and split-policy-driven unmatched-command escalation.

title: Route shell substitution through reviewable permission decisions with visible warnings
before: At parent commit 5ad5301805ef4aef2abc15596412c54e017c28eb, the permission manager and monitor tool could hard-deny commands containing $(), backticks, <(), or >(). In the permission manager, this happened only when surrounding rules caused full evaluation, so the same substitution could be approvable as a standalone command but denied inside a compound command with an unrelated matching rule. Hard denial also prevented YOLO-mode override. Some substitution shapes outside command AST nodes, and env-prefix substitutions removed by shell-wrapper stripping, could instead be misclassified as read-only and automatically allowed. Execution confirmations had no warnings contract or warning rendering.
after: At a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113, substitution-bearing agent shell and monitor commands are treated as non-read-only and normally resolve to ask rather than an implicit hard deny, while explicit deny rules retain precedence. Shell and monitor confirmations attach a shared informational warning for substitution, and the CLI renders warning-colored, prefixed text while reserving wrap-aware terminal height so approval options remain visible.

$(), backticks, <(), or >(). Two problems:

1. The deny couldn't be overridden by YOLO mode — YOLO sees the

This is the surviving half of a two-step migration. `fb7e30ad3
"fix(shell): remove command substitution deny check from

  AST read-only check already marks substitution-bearing commands as

  dialog renders these as ⚠-prefixed lines in the warning color,

candidate_workflows.name: replace-opaque-syntax-denial-with-informed-review
candidate_workflows.title: Replace inconsistent syntax denial with informed, policy-preserving review
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order workflow for moving a shell syntax hazard from an implicit hard-deny or accidental auto-allow state into a consistent approval path, with complete classification, visible context, and bounded confirmation UI.

workflow_graph.goal: Ensure a shell syntax risk is never denied merely by an inconsistent default branch or silently allowed through classifier gaps: it should require informed approval unless an explicit rule determines otherwise.
when_to_use: A shell-like tool has syntactic-risk checks duplicated across permission layers or sibling tools and equivalent commands receive different decisions depending on unrelated rules.
A permission fix that removes a hard deny could expose read-only-classification blind spots or lossy-normalization bypasses.
The approval surface needs to explain a risk while retaining usable controls in constrained layouts.
anti_goals: Do not weaken or override explicit user-configured deny rules.
Do not classify substitution-bearing commands as read-only merely to make them executable.
Do not apply the agent-tool approval policy to separately scoped user-authored shell-injection defenses.
Do not make warnings themselves errors or force ask when an explicit allow rule intentionally grants permission.
not_applicable_when: The syntax is prohibited by an explicit non-overridable product or sandbox policy rather than a default permission heuristic.
No approval mechanism exists and execution cannot be safely deferred to a user or configured policy.
The affected path is the separately scoped user-authored slash-command shell-injection path whose hard denial is an intentional prompt-injection defense.
inputs: Pinned implementation and parent refs
Permission-decision precedence and compound-command rules
All shell-like tool call sites using the classifier
Raw and normalized command representations
Primary AST and fallback read-only classifiers
Execution-confirmation data contract and renderers
Regression fixtures for syntax variants, wrappers, explicit rules, and constrained layouts
workflow_graph.entry_state: A risky shell construct can be implicitly hard-denied in selected evaluation paths, or can evade review when normalization/classification misses it; confirmation does not reliably communicate the risk.
workflow_graph.exit_state: All in-scope shell-like paths classify the construct as non-read-only, default to ask rather than deny, preserve explicit allow/deny semantics, attach consistent warning context when confirmation occurs, and keep warnings plus approval controls visible.

steps.condition: The hard-deny removal depends on the read-only classifier being the safety gate.
steps.validation: Prove that raw-only wrapper prefixes, quoted wrapper bodies, non-command AST nodes, and fallback parsing all remain non-read-only.

steps.condition: An approval path exists and explicit rule decisions remain authoritative.
steps.validation: Standalone and compound implicit-risk cases return ask; read-only controls return allow; explicit matching denials still return deny.

steps.condition: The command reaches a confirmation-producing interactive shell-like path.
steps.validation: All supported risk syntaxes attach the shared warning and a plain command omits warnings.

steps.condition: The confirmation consumer is a height-constrained terminal UI.
steps.validation: Warning text, command truncation, and every approval choice remain visible in a tight compact fixture; warning-free confirmations retain prior behavior.

validation_ladder: Unit-test the shared raw/stripped detection and warning helper with positive and negative commands.
Test primary AST and fallback classification for assignments, redirects, wrappers, and every supported substitution syntax.
Test permission decisions for standalone input, compound commands with unrelated matching rules, sibling tools, read-only controls, and explicit deny precedence.
Test confirmation producers for warning presence and absence.
Render interactive confirmations under ordinary, narrow, and compact height constraints and verify both warning and choices.
Run the affected multi-package regression suite and strict TypeScript build.
stop_conditions: Stop if explicit deny precedence is lost or an implicit-risk command becomes allow through any primary or fallback path.
Stop if raw and normalized detection disagree without a documented, tested reason.
Stop if a confirmation consumer cannot represent the warning without hiding or removing user choices.
Defer surfaces governed by a different threat model instead of applying the agent-tool policy indiscriminately.
unresolved_or_deferred: The issue bundle lacks GitHub discussion, review, and status-check metadata; review rationale is available only through the pinned commit message.
The pinned commit intentionally leaves checkCommandPermissions hard-denial behavior for user-authored !{...} shell injections unchanged because that path has a distinct prompt-injection threat model.

Warning propagation to ACP and non-interactive consumers was explicitly removed as out of scope in the final commit, so this workflow grounds only the retained interactive shell and monitor confirmation surfaces.

unresolved_questions: The recorded 1,262-test and strict-build result comes from the pinned commit message; this extraction did not independently rerun that full validation suite.

Several changed CLI completion, directory-command, and provider files appear to be accompanying integration or branch-history changes and were not used to infer the permission-policy workflow because the inspected permission implementation and tests provide the direct resolution boundary.
